title: Wages
description: Qualified wages are taxable wages paid to employees for conducting, directly supervising or directly supporting qualified research under IRC Section 41.

body.text: Qualified wages are taxable wages subject to income tax withholding under IRC § 3401(a) paid to employees for qualified services—conducting, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research—under the U.S. Section 41 R&D tax credit. They make up about 69% of claimed qualified research expenses, and 100% of wages count when at least 80% of an employee's service time qualifies.

Qualified Wages (QWs) constitute the single largest expenditure category within the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, accounting for approximately 69% of all claimed Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) nationwide—and 70.66% among corporate filers electing the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC)—according to U.S. Department of the Treasury Office of Tax Analysis and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Statistics of Income (SOI) corporate return data. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and § 41(b)(2)(D)(i)–(iii), employee remuneration qualifies as an in-house research expense only if it satisfies a strict two-part statutory filter: first, the compensation must constitute "wages" subject to federal income tax withholding at the source under Chapter 24, 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) (or earned income of self-employed individuals under IRC § 401(c)(2), while excluding non-taxable fringe benefits, employer qualified retirement plan contributions, pre-tax IRC § 125 cafeteria plan salary reductions, pre-tax IRC § 402(e)(3) elective deferrals, and any wages taken into account in computing the Work Opportunity Credit under IRC § 51(a)); second, those wages must be paid or incurred for "qualified services" performed by the employee within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or a U.S. possession. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), qualified services are bounded by three mutually exclusive functional pillars: (1) engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, (2) engaging in the immediate, first-line direct supervision of qualified research, or (3) engaging in the direct support of qualified research.

When an employee performs both qualified and nonqualified services during a taxable year, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) restricts the claimable in-house research expense to the fraction of IRC § 3401(a) wages attributable to active service hours spent on qualified services, excluding non-working paid time off (such as sick leave, vacation, and paid holidays) from the denominator. However, under the statutory and regulatory "substantially all" safe harbor of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80% of an individual employee's active service time during the taxable year consists of qualified services—evaluated strictly on an employee-by-employee basis—100% of that employee's annual IRC § 3401(a) wages qualify as QREs. Because wage allocations dominate total QRE dollars, IRS examinations focus heavily on the "hybrid/nexus problem," routinely disallowing claims that multiply departmental Form W-2 cost-center totals by uncorroborated, retrospective percentage estimates from Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) without contemporaneous activity-level documentation tying employee hours to business components that satisfy all four elements of IRC § 41(d)(1).

items: Form 6765 Section G Mandatory Effective Date Deferred to Tax Year 2026: Following stakeholder feedback on earlier drafts that had proposed a 2025 mandate, the IRS issued News Release IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025) and published the finalized Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, released in February 2026), making Section G (Business Component Information, including Columns 50–53 disaggregated wage reporting) optional for all filers on original returns for tax years beginning before 2026 (covering both 2024 and 2025 original returns) and mandatory only for tax years beginning after 2025 (starting on or after January 1, 2026, for the 2027 filing season), subject to exemptions for Qualified Small Business (QSB) payroll-tax-credit electors and small filers on original returns with controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less and prior three-year average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less.

Equity Compensation Withholding Distinctions Between NSOs and ISOs: While Non-Qualified Stock Option (NSO) exercise spreads are subject to federal income tax withholding under IRC § 3401(a) upon exercise and qualify as QRE wages in the exercise year if the employee performed qualified services in the grant year (Apple Computer, Inc. v. Commissioner, 98 T.C. 232 (1992)), Congress amended 26 U.S.C. § 421(b) and § 423(c) in Pub. L. 108-357 (2004) to specify that no amount is required to be deducted and withheld under Chapter 24 (§ 3401(a)) upon a disqualifying disposition of Incentive Stock Option (ISO) or Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) shares, even though the resulting ordinary income is reported on Form W-2.

Qualifying Research-Specific Clerical Work vs. Excluded General Administration: Contrary to overly broad assertions that secretarial or clerical tasks are categorically disqualified, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) and the IRS June 2005 Audit Techniques Guide explicitly include "the services of a secretary for typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research" and "of a clerk for compiling research data" as qualifying direct support, while excluding general and administrative (G&A) services such as payroll preparation, accounting for research costs, or general janitorial cleaning.

Appellate Clarification of Little Sandy Coal on Direct Support and Production Wages: On appeal in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the Seventh Circuit affirmed complete disallowance of claimed research credits due to uncorroborated shortcut wage estimates, but explicitly rejected the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of direct support and production worker activities from the numerator of the 80% process-of-experimentation fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Distinction Between Refund Claim Intake Screening (CCM 20214101F) and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson: Secondary consultancy articles occasionally attribute upfront IRS Classifier intake rejections of amended-return refund claims to Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner (or misstate its Tax Court citation as T.C. Memo. 2022-127, which is actually Kechijian v. Commissioner, an unrelated IRC § 6015 innocent spouse decision). Primary judicial records confirm that Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 7805-16 (T.C.), aff'd, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024) (No. 23-1523), was an examination deficiency case decided on summary judgment under the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) "funded research" exclusion, whereas upfront sufficiency screening of amended-return refund claims is governed by IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum (CCM) 20214101F, whose 45-day perfection transition period was extended through January 10, 2027, by IR-2025-99.

body.text: I. Executive Summary: Strategic Weight and Compliance Risk of Qualified Wages
A. Empirical Share of Qualified Wages in Total QREs

Qualified Wages represent the primary financial driver of the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC § 41. While secondary payroll and tax advisory blogs routinely state that employee wages represent "70% or more" of total QREs without publishing underlying statistical tables, primary federal tax return data compiled by the U.S. Department of the Treasury Office of Tax Analysis (OTA) and the IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) division substantiates this benchmark. In its October 12, 2016 report analyzing corporate Form 6765 filings (Research and Experimentation (R&E) Credit, presenting Tax Year 2012 IRS SOI corporate return tabulations), the Treasury Department documented that wages and salaries paid for qualified services account for approximately 69% of aggregate QRE spending across all corporate claimants, whereas supplies account for 15%, contract research expenses account for 16%, and computer rental or lease costs account for a negligible percentage (less than 1%) of total QREs.

Among corporations electing the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method—which represented 51% of corporate claimants and 69% of aggregate corporate QRE dollars in the Tax Year 2012 Treasury SOI tabulation, compared to 31% of QRE dollars reported under the Regular Credit method—qualified wages accounted for $99,413,316 thousand out of $140,687,454 thousand in total ASC QREs, or 70.66%, alongside $21,991,435 thousand (15.63%) in applicable contract research expenses. Earlier longitudinal IRS SOI panel data from the credit's first decade (1981–1991) similarly documented that in-house qualified wages constituted 66.6% of total QREs. Across software engineering, technology, and professional engineering firms where tangible raw material consumption is low relative to technical human capital, the concentration of QREs on the wage line is frequently even higher.
B. The Nexus Mandate and Escalating IRS Scrutiny

Because employee compensation dominates the QRE base, the accounting and engineering methodology used to identify, quantify, and allocate wages directly governs both the magnitude of a taxpayer's credit and its vulnerability to IRS examination adjustments and 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662. As documented in the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG, LMSB-04-0508-030, published May 2008), a primary driver of audit disallowances is the "hybrid/nexus problem"—the inability of a taxpayer to establish an auditable, evidentiary connection between financial accounting and payroll records (such as Form W-2 wage registers aggregated by organizational department or cost center) and the specific underlying research projects and qualified activities performed. Taxpayers routinely create this exposure by extracting departmental W-2 pools after year-end and multiplying them by retrospective percentage estimates obtained from managers or Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) months or years after the tax year closes, falling short of the recordkeeping mandate of IRC § 6001.

Both the IRS and the federal courts require taxpayers to substantiate a direct nexus establishing that claimed wage dollars compensated services supporting specific business components that satisfy all four elements of the statutory test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2):

items: The Section 174 / Section 174A Domestic Research Expenditure Test: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) (as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, coordinating with newly enacted IRC § 174A alongside § 174 and 26 CFR § 1.174-2), the expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures incurred in the taxpayer's trade or business (and reasonable in amount under IRC § 174(e)) to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a product or process, or the appropriate design of that product or process, based on information available at the outset of the activity.

The Discovering Technological Information Test: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii), the research activity must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

The Business Component Test: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(B), the application of that technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component—defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer—evaluated separately for each component (subject to the "shrinking-back" rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) where subcomponent-level documentation is maintained).

The Process of Experimentation Test: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), § 41(d)(3), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), substantially all (at least 80%, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis without regard to 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)) of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation—evaluating alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error—for a qualified purpose (new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, rather than style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors).

body.text: II. Foundational Legal Framework: Defining Wages and Qualified Services
A. Statutory Definition of Wages (IRC Section 41(b)(2)(D) and IRC Section 3401(a))

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1)(A) and § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), a taxpayer's "in-house research expenses" encompass "any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee". Rather than creating a standalone research-credit compensation definition, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i) incorporates the federal income tax withholding definition at the source: "The term 'wages' has the meaning given such term by section 3401(a)". Under Chapter 24 of the Internal Revenue Code, 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) and 26 CFR § 31.3401(a)-1(a) define "wages" as "all remuneration (other than fees paid to a public official) for services performed by an employee for his employer, including the cash value of all remuneration (including benefits) paid in any medium other than cash," except as specifically excluded under paragraphs (1) through (23) of § 3401(a) or § 3402(e).

Two statutory rules in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii)–(iii) modify this baseline. First, for sole proprietors, partners, and other self-employed individuals or owner-employees treated as employees within the meaning of IRC § 401(c)(1), 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii) expands "wages" to include the individual's "earned income" as defined in IRC § 401(c)(2), to the extent allocable to qualified services performed by that individual. Conversely, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii) imposes an explicit anti-double-benefit exclusion: "The term 'wages' shall not include any amount taken into account in determining the work opportunity credit under section 51(a)".
1. Includible Compensation Components and Stock Option Rules

As confirmed in Section 4(a) of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41 — Qualified Research Expenses (published June 2005), IRC § 3401(a) wages generally correspond to taxable employee compensation subject to federal income tax withholding and reported on Form W-2, Box 1. Includible remuneration encompasses regular base salaries, hourly wages, overtime pay, paid vacation allowances (which 26 CFR § 31.3401(a)-1(b)(3) explicitly defines as statutory "wages" notwithstanding the employee's absence from work), dismissal payments, taxable cash performance bonuses, and nonqualified deferred compensation includible in gross income under the flush language of IRC § 3401(a) and IRC § 409A.

Employee stock option exercises require a careful legal distinction between Non-Qualified Stock Options (NSOs) and statutory stock options—Incentive Stock Options (ISOs) under IRC § 422(b) and Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) options under IRC § 423(b)—coupled with a two-period tracing analysis across the grant year and the exercise year. In Apple Computer, Inc. v. Commissioner, 98 T.C. 232 (1992), acq., 1992-2 C.B. 1, the U.S. Tax Court held that the spread income realized upon an employee's exercise of an NSO (the excess of the stock's fair market value at exercise over the option exercise price) constitutes IRC § 3401(a) wages subject to withholding and therefore qualifies as wages under IRC § 41. Incorporating Apple Computer, Section 4(a) of the IRS June 2005 ATG instructs examiners that because an option is granted as compensation for work performed in an earlier period, eligibility requires looking back to the grant year to determine whether the employee performed "qualified services". (While one sentence in the 2005 ATG loosely states that an option is "subject to withholding upon grant," NSO spreads are withheld upon exercise and reported on Form W-2, and the ATG immediately clarifies that if the work performed in the grant year qualified, "the spread amount is included in wages in the year the option is exercised".)

By contrast, statutory stock options (ISOs and IRC § 423 ESPP options) result in no taxable income and no Chapter 24 withholding at the time of exercise under 26 U.S.C. § 421(a). Under pre-2004 law in Sun Microsystems, Inc. v. Commissioner (cited with IRS acquiescence in the June 2005 ATG), the Tax Court held that when an employee subsequently made a "disqualifying disposition" of ISO stock under IRC § 421(b) (disposing of shares within two years from option grant or within one year after share transfer), the resulting spread income constituted IRC § 3401(a) wages for IRC § 41 credit purposes. However, in Pub. L. 108-357 (2004), Congress amended 26 U.S.C. § 421(b) and § 423(c) by adding the explicit statutory sentence: "No amount shall be required to be deducted and withheld under chapter 24 with respect to any increase in income attributable to a disposition described in the preceding sentence". Consequently, although ordinary compensation income from a post-2004 disqualifying disposition of ISO or ESPP shares is reported on the employee's Form W-2, it is statutorily exempt from Chapter 24 (§ 3401(a)) withholding, creating a critical divergence from NSO exercise spreads that taxpayers must account for when filtering W-2 payroll data under the IRS ATG's "subject to withholding" standard.
2. Excluded Compensation Components and the W-2 vs. Section 3401(a) Nuance

A frequent compliance error in R&D credit studies is substituting "total labor cost" or "gross compensation" from general ledger payroll accounts for statutory IRC § 3401(a) wages. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(i) and Section 4(a) of the IRS June 2005 ATG, any remuneration not subject to federal income tax withholding under IRC § 3401(a) is excluded from Qualified Wages, even if paid to a full-time research scientist. This excludes employer 401(k) matches and qualified retirement plan contributions under 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a)(12)(A)–(E), employee pre-tax 401(k) elective deferrals under IRC § 402(e)(3), employee pre-tax salary reductions under an IRC § 125 cafeteria plan (such as pre-tax health insurance premiums and flexible spending account deductions, as confirmed in IRS Chief Counsel Advice 201622031 and IRS Publication 15-B), and non-taxable statutory fringe benefits under IRC §§ 106, 127, 129, and 132 and § 3401(a)(18)–(22).

Furthermore, tax practitioners must verify exact alignment between Form W-2, Box 1 and strict IRC § 3401(a) wages. Certain imputed income items included as taxable compensation in Form W-2, Box 1—specifically the taxable cost of employer-provided group-term life insurance coverage exceeding $50,000 under IRC § 79—are statutorily exempt from Chapter 24 income tax withholding under 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a)(14). Pulling unadjusted Form W-2, Box 1 totals without removing § 3401(a)(14) imputed group-term life insurance, § 421(b) / § 423(c) statutory option disposition income exempt from Chapter 24 withholding, and § 51(a) Work Opportunity Credit wages can therefore overstate permissible IRC § 41 wages.

body.text: B. Definition of Qualified Services (The Three Pillars)

Satisfying the IRC § 3401(a) wage definition is a necessary but insufficient condition for QRE inclusion. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1), employee wages constitute in-house research expenses only to the extent paid or incurred for "qualified services" performed by the employee. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i)–(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), qualified services are divided into three distinct operational pillars—which correspond directly to Columns 50, 51, and 52 of redesigned Form 6765, Section G.
1. Engaging in Qualified Research (Actual Conduct)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1), "engaging in qualified research" means the actual conduct of qualified research, illustrated in the regulation by "a scientist conducting laboratory experiments". In operational practice, actual conduct encompasses hands-on execution of the technical experimentation process: engineers designing and testing physical or digital prototypes, software developers writing and debugging experimental algorithms, and laboratory scientists executing iterative trials to resolve technological uncertainty. On Form 6765, wages for actual conduct are reported by business component in Section G, Column 50 ("Direct research wages for qualified services").
2. Direct Supervision of Qualified Research

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research, illustrated by "a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments, but who may not actually perform experiments". Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) imposes a strict hierarchical cutoff: "'Direct supervision' does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist".

As Section 4(a) of the IRS June 2005 ATG emphasizes, eligibility determinations turn on what an employee actually does rather than corporate titles or generic position descriptions. Higher-level managers—such as Vice Presidents of Engineering, Chief Technology Officers, or Directors to whom first-line managers report—cannot claim general managerial or executive oversight of first-line supervisors. While such executives may occasionally perform minor fractions of hands-on qualified research or direct technical supervision of bench researchers due to their scientific expertise, only that specific, documented fraction of their service hours may be claimed. Federal courts enforce this substantiation standard strictly: as noted in case law analyses of T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (affirmed by the Seventh Circuit on April 30, 2024), payroll records establishing a company president's and chief operating officer's compensation failed to sustain any research credit where the taxpayer lacked evidence proving the time devoted to qualifying technical services. Reflecting IRS scrutiny of executive compensation, Form 6765 requires direct supervision wages to be reported by business component in Section G, Column 51, and mandates that every claimant separately disclose on Section E, Line 38 the total amount of officers' wages (determined under the laws of the state of incorporation, regardless of shareholder status) included on Section F, Line 42. (Tax practitioners have observed that while the Form 6765 instructions reference "the corporation" and state incorporation law in defining officers, non-corporate entities should carefully document any executive compensation included in QREs pending further IRS guidance.)
3. Direct Support of Qualified Research and the Clerical/Secretarial Distinction

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3), "direct support" means services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3), direct support does not include supervision; supervisory services constitute qualified services solely to the extent provided in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2).

A recurring misconception in secondary R&D credit literature is asserting that secretarial or clerical staff are categorically excluded from direct support. In fact, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) and Section 4(a) of the IRS June 2005 ATG draw a functional line between research-specific support tasks and general administrative services, explicitly providing four examples of qualifying direct support: (1) the services of a secretary for typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research; (2) the services of a laboratory worker for cleaning equipment used in qualified research; (3) the services of a clerk for compiling research data; and (4) the services of a machinist for machining a part of an experimental model used in qualified research.

Conversely, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) excludes general administrative services, or other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities—explicitly specifying that this exclusion applies whether general administrative personnel are part of the research department or in a separate department. Specifically, payroll personnel preparing salary checks of laboratory scientists, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, and corporate officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel matters do not qualify as direct support of research. On Form 6765, qualifying direct support wages are reported by business component in Section G, Column 52.
C. Excluded Activities and Geographic Restrictions (IRC Section 41(d)(4))

Even when performed by scientists or engineers inside an R&D department, employee hours spent on statutorily excluded activities under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c) cannot be counted as qualified services. In particular, practitioners must apply the exact statutory geographic scope of the foreign research exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F): rather than restricting eligible services solely to the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia, IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) disqualifies only research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States. Consequently, wages paid for qualified services physically performed within the 50 states, D.C., Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions are geographically eligible, whereas wages for research conducted in foreign countries are excluded even if paid by a domestic U.S. employer on a Form W-2 to a U.S. citizen.

body.text: III. Wage Allocation Methodology: The Substantially All Rule (The 80% Test)
A. Mechanics of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2)

When an employee performs both qualified services and nonqualified services during a taxable year, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) establishes the general fractional allocation rule: only the amount of wages allocated to the performance of qualified services constitutes an in-house research expense. In the absence of another method of allocation that the taxpayer can demonstrate to be more appropriate, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) directs that the includible wage expense be determined by multiplying the employee's total annual IRC § 3401(a) wages by a time-based Qualified Services Ratio (QSR):

However, the flush language of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) establish a statutory and regulatory safe harbor known as the "substantially all" rule (or the 80% cliff). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), if the wages allocated (on the time basis used under § 1.41-2(d)(1)) to services meeting IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii) constitute at least 80% of the wages paid to or incurred for the employee during the taxable year, then "substantially all" of the employee's services are treated as qualified services, and 100% of that employee's IRC § 3401(a) wages for the taxable year qualify as in-house research expenses. Conversely, if the employee's QSR is less than 80%, the "substantially all" safe harbor does not apply, and only the exact fractional percentage of IRC § 3401(a) wages corresponding to the employee's QSR may be claimed. As Section 4(a) of the IRS June 2005 ATG emphasizes, the 80% test under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) is evaluated strictly on an employee-by-employee basis, never as a department-wide or group average.

Practitioners must also strictly separate the two distinct 80% "substantially all" rules in IRC § 41. First, at the business-component level, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) require that at least 80% of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose—and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) explicitly states that this business-component test is determined "without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2)". Only after each business component independently satisfies § 1.41-4(a)(6) are an individual employee's hours across qualifying business components aggregated and evaluated under the employee-level 80% rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) to determine whether 100% or only a fractional share of that employee's IRC § 3401(a) wages enters QREs.
B. Denominator Precision: Excluding Non-Service Paid Time Off (PTO)
A decisive technical requirement in computing each employee's QSR under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) and the IRS June 2005 ATG governs the denominator of the allocation fraction:

Because 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) measures "the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year," compensated hours for which an employee is paid but is not performing services must be excluded from both the numerator and the denominator. Section 4(a) of the IRS June 2005 ATG explicitly notes that "sick leave, for example, would not be included in the fraction". By the same regulatory principle under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1), vacation leave, paid holidays, jury duty, bereavement leave, and military leave—during which no services are performed—are excluded from the denominator. Because paid vacation allowances and taxable sick pay constitute statutory IRC § 3401(a) wages under 26 CFR § 31.3401(a)-1(b)(3), excluding non-service PTO hours from the QSR denominator ensures that the employee's active service ratio allocates their entire annual IRC § 3401(a) wage base rather than penalizing paid leave as non-qualified labor.

Hypothetical Worked Example 1 (Impact of PTO Denominator Adjustment): Consider a full-time salaried research engineer paid for a standard 2,080-hour work year (assuming a $100,000.00 unit IRC § 3401(a) wage base), whose payroll register includes 200 hours of non-service PTO (vacation, holidays, and sick leave), and who logs 1,500 hours performing qualified services. If the taxpayer erroneously uses unadjusted paid hours (2,080) as the denominator, the resulting ratio is 1,500 / 2,080 = 72.1154% (72.12%), yielding $72,115.38 in claimable wages and understating the employee's actual service allocation by 7.67 percentage points. Conversely, when the taxpayer properly subtracts the 200 non-service PTO hours per 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) and the IRS ATG to establish 2,080 − 200 = 1,880 Total Service Hours, dividing 1,500 qualified service hours by 1,880 total service hours yields 79.7872% (79.79%), increasing claimable fractional wages by +$7,671.85 to $79,787.23. While 79.79% remains 0.21 percentage points—exactly 4 qualified service hours (0.80 × 1,880 = 1,504 hours)—shy of the 80.00% threshold, proper denominator modeling reveals during a mid-year review that reallocating just 4 hours of routine administrative tasks away from this engineer would legitimately cross the 80% cliff and unlock the remaining +$20,212.77 of annual wages for 100% ($100,000.00) capture.
C. Hypothetical Worked Examples: Recomputing the 80% Cliff Across Engineering Roles

To demonstrate the exact arithmetic sensitivity of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), three canonical engineering compensation scenarios illustrate how minor shifts in active duty allocation affect QRE totals.

In Scenario 1 (Senior Mechanical Engineer — Case A vs. Case B), assume a Senior Mechanical Engineer receives $130,000.00 in strict IRC § 3401(a) taxable W-2 wages during a 2,080-hour paid year that includes 160 hours of paid vacation and holidays, resulting in 2,080 − 160 = 1,920 Total Service Hours. In Case A, the engineer logs 1,550 hours of qualified services, yielding a QSR of 1,550 / 1,920 = 80.7292% (80.73%). Because 80.73% is at least 80%, the "substantially all" rule applies and 100% ($130,000.00) of the engineer's IRC § 3401(a) wages qualify as QREs—$25,052.08 higher than the straight pro-rata value of $104,947.92 ($130,000.00 × 1,550 / 1,920). In Case B, the identical engineer logs 1,450 hours of qualified services (100 hours fewer than Case A), yielding a QSR of 1,450 / 1,920 = 75.5208% (75.52%). Because 75.52% is below 80%, only the fractional allocation qualifies. Multiplying $130,000.00 by the unrounded fraction (1,450 / 1,920) yields $98,177.08—a reduction of $31,822.92 compared to Case A—while multiplying $130,000.00 by the rounded two-decimal percentage (75.52%) yields $98,176.00, a reduction of $31,824.00. Thus, a 5.21 percentage-point drop in qualified hours triggers a 24.48% reduction in claimable Qualified Wages.

In Scenario 2 (Senior Software Developer "Alex"), a Senior Software Developer earning $150,000.00 in IRC § 3401(a) wages spends 85.00% of total service hours coding and testing new software features (qualified services) and 15.00% in general administrative meetings (non-qualified services). Crossing the 80% threshold allows the taxpayer to include 100% ($150,000.00) in QREs rather than the straight pro-rata $127,500.00 (0.85 × $150,000.00), capturing an additional +$22,500.00 in qualified wages. Conversely, in Scenario 3 (Baseline Simulator Engineer — 75% QSR), an engineer receiving $100,000.00 in IRC § 3401(a) wages who spends 75.00% of active service hours on R&D falls below the 80% threshold and is limited strictly to the pro-rata amount of $75,000.00 (0.75 × $100,000.00).

body.text: IV. Documentation, Judicial Precedent, and Audit Defense
A. The IRS Position on the Hybrid/Nexus Problem and SME Estimates

In the May 2008 Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG, LMSB-04-0508-030) and IRS Chief Counsel Field Attorney Advice 20171601F, the IRS distinguishes between two primary accounting methodologies for capturing QREs: the Project Method, which tracks labor and direct expenses directly to individual research projects and naturally establishes nexus, and the Cost Center Method, which accumulates expenses by organizational department. Because departmental cost-center ledgers rarely isolate qualified research from routine operations, many taxpayers and third-party credit consultants construct a Hybrid Method—adopting whichever portions of each system have readily available records by extracting W-2 wage totals by cost center and multiplying individual or department-wide wages by a "qualified percentage" obtained from interviews or questionnaires completed by Subject Matter Experts (SMEs).

The RCCATG warns examiners that hybrid studies typically fail to substantiate the relationship between accounting records and underlying qualified research activities—creating a fatal nexus problem that violates IRC § 6001 recordkeeping rules and renders the study "not auditable". Under the RCCATG, examiners are instructed to reject arbitrary or unsupported wage allocation percentages and disallow part or all of claimed cost-center QREs when SMEs opining on employee time allocations did not actually work in the relevant areas or perform services for the taxpayer during the tax years at issue; when SME memory-based recollections of time spent on qualified, excluded, or nonqualified activities are unsupported by measurable, corroborative records; when a single blanket estimated percentage is applied across an entire department's total wage pool rather than evaluated on an individual employee-by-employee and business-component-by-business-component basis; or when the taxpayer maintained an internal project time-tracking methodology in its business operations yet chose not to use it when preparing its research credit claim.
B. Judicial Precedent: Inseparability of Technical Proof and Wage Substantiation

Recent federal court decisions confirm that wage substantiation cannot be divorced from technical and contractual substantiation of the underlying business component under IRC § 41(d). Even where payroll records are undisputed, if a taxpayer fails to demonstrate that a business component satisfies all four elements of IRC § 41(d)(1)—or fails to overcome a statutory exclusion—none of the employee wages associated with that component qualify as QREs.
1. Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024)

In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22, opinion issued December 23, 2024), the U.S. Tax Court evaluated R&D tax credits claimed by a mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) consulting engineering firm for tax years 2013 through 2016 (utilized across 2015–2019). The parties tried a sample of three building design projects: the Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit, Baptist Memorial Hospital–North Mississippi (Oxford), and the Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building.

The Tax Court disallowed 100% of the claimed credits across all three sampled projects and upheld 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662. On the Section 174 uncertainty test, the court held that performing standard engineering calculations using historical data and known formulas (such as calculating duct size from airflow) or not knowing a building's initial footprint did not establish that available information failed to establish capability, method, or appropriate design at the outset. Similarly, the firm's standard six-stage design process (Basis of Design, Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Bidding, and Construction Administration) was linear rather than an evaluative, hypothesis-driven process of experimentation. Crucially for wage compliance, although the engineering firm submitted employee timesheets, the Tax Court held that those timesheets failed to substantiate qualified wages because they lacked activity-level detail connecting specific engineer hours to an evaluative process of experimentation. Because the record also lacked granular subcomponent documentation, the court could not apply the "shrinking-back rule" under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to preserve any subset of engineering wages.
2. Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (2021), aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)

In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (decided February 11, 2021), aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. March 7, 2023), the taxpayer's shipbuilding subsidiary, Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS), claimed $1,141,713 in research credits for the tax year ended June 30, 2014, based on production wages, nonproduction engineering and management wages, and supplies incurred in building two representative vessels: the Apex Tanker (Project 720) and a floating dry dock (Project 730).

Both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit disallowed the claimed credits in full, clarifying the relationship between the 80% process-of-experimentation test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)) and employee wage claims. First, both courts rejected the taxpayer's argument that because 80% to 90% of the physical hull and vessel components were novel or redesigned compared to prior vessels, the projects satisfied the "substantially all" (80%) process-of-experimentation requirement; 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) measures research activities, not the physical proportion of novel product elements. Second, in T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the Tax Court had reasoned that under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), individuals providing direct supervision or direct support (including production workers fabricating physical components of a pilot model) are not "engaged in" qualified research, and therefore their activities could never be included in the numerator of the 80% process-of-experimentation fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6). On appeal, however, the Seventh Circuit (62 F.4th 287) explicitly rejected the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of direct support and production activities, clarifying that production activities can constitute elements of a process of experimentation when properly substantiated—a rule subsequently applied by the Tax Court in Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner (Docket No. 11019-19, April 2024 order denying IRS summary judgment on production expenses). Despite correcting the Tax Court's legal rule on direct support and production wages, the Seventh Circuit affirmed complete disallowance in Little Sandy Coal because the taxpayer did not track nonproduction or production employee hours by experimental activity, relying instead on arbitrary, after-the-fact "shortcut estimates" that failed to establish that at least 80% of research activities were experimental. (Subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence, including George v. Commissioner, has continued to penalize broad retroactive wage estimates while clarifying that substantiated trial supply expenses can still qualify independently of wage QREs.)
3. IRS Refund Claim Intake Screening (CCM 20214101F) vs. Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Funded Research

Taxpayers must also distinguish between substantive funded-research disallowances during examination and administrative intake screening of amended-return refund claims. Secondary consultancy articles have occasionally attributed IRS Classifier intake rejections of refund claims to Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner (2024), while other secondary commentary cites the underlying Tax Court decision in that case as T.C. Memo. 2022-127. Primary judicial records clarify both points: T.C. Memo. 2022-127 (filed December 28, 2022, Docket No. 3430-20) is Kechijian v. Commissioner, an unrelated IRC § 6015 innocent spouse relief decision. In Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 7805-16 (T.C.), aff'd, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024) (No. 23-1523), the Tax Court (on summary judgment) and the Eighth Circuit resolved an examination deficiency dispute in which a Minnesota structural engineering firm claimed approximately $190,000 in research credits across fiscal years ended September 30, 2010, 2011, and 2013. Examining 14 representative contracts, the Eighth Circuit disallowed all claimed credits under the funded research exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1) because client payments were conditioned on professional service completion rather than successful research outcomes, exposing the firm only to general economic risk. On June 16, 2026, the Tax Court reinforced this two-part funding analysis in Smith v. Commissioner (T.C. Nos. 13382-17 et al.)—rejecting a Loper Bright challenge to the § 41 regulations, holding that an architectural partnership lacked "substantial rights" under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) in two of six sampled projects and faced funding reductions on the remaining four, while separately holding that disputed partner compensation satisfied the reasonable-compensation requirement of IRC § 174(e).

Upfront IRS Classifier intake screening of research credit refund claims on amended returns is governed separately by IRS Office of Chief Counsel Memorandum (CCM) 20214101F (issued October 2021) and updated refund sufficiency rules. For refund claims postmarked after June 18, 2024, taxpayers must provide at the time of filing: (1) identification of all business components to which the IRC § 41 claim relates for that tax year; (2) a description of all research activities performed for each business component; and (3) the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which taxpayers can satisfy via Form 6765 or an acceptable schedule containing the required details). Under IRS News Release IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS extended the refund-claim transition period through January 10, 2027, granting taxpayers 45 days to perfect a deficient amended-return refund claim upon receiving an IRS notice before final rejection.
V. Reporting Qualified Wages on IRS Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2024 / Jan. 2025 and Instructions Rev. Dec. 2025)
A. Aggregated Entity-Level Reporting: Section F, Line 42, Section E, Line 38, and Section 280C Coordination

Taxpayers compute and report the Credit for Increasing Research Activities on redesigned IRS Form 6765 (released with a Rev. December 2024 form header on February 11, 2025, and referenced as the January 2025 revision in the finalized Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) released on February 6, 2026). At the top of Page 1, Item A requires taxpayers on an original timely filed return (including extensions) to check "Yes" or "No" to make or decline the reduced credit election under IRC § 280C(c)(2). Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1), as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 (§ 70302(b)(2)(B)) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, if a taxpayer checks "No" on Item A to claim the full credit under IRC § 41(a), its domestic research or experimental expenditures as defined in IRC § 174A(b) (including qualified R&D wages) otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to capital account must be reduced by the amount of the allowed IRC § 41(a) credit.

Under the revamped form layout, QRE category breakouts are removed from Section A (Regular Credit) and Section B (Alternative Simplified Credit) and consolidated into Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary), which is mandatory for all claimants starting with the 2024 tax year. Aggregate Qualified Wages are reported on Section F, Line 42: "Total wages for qualified services for all business components (do not include any wages used in figuring the work opportunity credit)". Line 42 combines with supplies (Line 43), computer rental or lease costs (Line 44), and applicable contract and basic research amounts (Line 47) to produce total QREs on Line 48, which is carried to Line 5 or Line 20. When Section G is completed, Section F, Line 42 equals the grand total of Section G, Column 53 across all reported business components.

Three strict entity-level rules govern wage reporting across Sections E and F. First, under IRC § 41(f)(1) and the finalized Form 6765 Instructions (incorporating the IRS's June 2025 controlled-group clarification), if the filing taxpayer is a member of a controlled group of corporations or group of trades or businesses under common control and files a separate tax return, the member must enter on Section F, Line 42 only that individual member's own qualified wages—never the combined controlled group amount of qualified wages (even though group-level QREs are entered for prior base years on Line 26 and used to evaluate controlled-group thresholds). Second, every taxpayer reporting QREs on Line 48 must complete Section E (Other Information), entering on Line 37 the total number of business components generating the QREs on Line 5 or Line 20. Third, on Section E, Line 38, the taxpayer must separately report the dollar amount of officers' wages included on Line 42, with officer status determined under the laws of the state of incorporation regardless of whether an officer is also a shareholder.
B. Component-Level Wage Reporting: Section G, Columns 50–53 and Effective Dates
1. Mandatory Effective Date (Tax Year 2026) and Small-Taxpayer Exemptions

Although early IRS draft instructions released in late 2024 and January 2025 had proposed making Section G (Business Component Information) mandatory for tax years beginning after 2024, the IRS issued News Release IR-2025-99 on October 1, 2025, and published the finalized Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) in February 2026, deferring mandatory implementation by one full year.

Under IR-2025-99 and the Rev. December 2025 Instructions, for tax years beginning before 2026 (including both 2024 and 2025 original returns), completion of Section G is optional for all filers. For tax years beginning after 2025 (starting on or after January 1, 2026, processed in the 2027 filing season), Section G is mandatory for all filers (indicated via Question A at the top of Section F), except for two categories of taxpayers for whom Section G remains optional. First, Section G is optional for a Qualified Small Business (QSB) under IRC § 41(h)(3) (a corporation, including an S corporation, or partnership—or other non-exempt person aggregating gross receipts across all trades or businesses, excluding IRC § 501 tax-exempt organizations—with less than $5 million in gross receipts for the credit year and zero gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with the credit year) that checks the box on Section D, Line 33a to elect to claim a portion of its research credit (up to $500,000 on Line 34, carried to Form 8974) as a payroll tax credit; a QSB that does not check Line 33a is not exempt. Second, Section G is optional under the small-filer exception for taxpayers claiming the research credit on an original filed return whose controlled-group QREs on Line 48 are $1.5 million or less AND whose average annual gross receipts for the prior 3 tax years are $50 million or less, determined at the controlled group level under IRC § 448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph (A). Amended returns are not eligible for this exemption; taxpayers claiming an increased research credit on an amended return (including for a 2025 tax year) must provide the required business-component disclosures (including Column 49(f) when using Section G) under the amended-return refund claim rules.
2. The 80% / Top 50 Business Component Rule and Columns 50–53 Wage Breakdown

When completing Section G, taxpayers must report business components in descending order of QRE amount until the itemized components represent a minimum of 80% of total QREs reported on Line 48, up to a maximum of 50 business components (the "80%/Top 50" rule). Any remaining components beyond the 80%/Top 50 threshold are combined on a single row by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) and reporting their aggregated QREs across Columns 50 through 56. Taxpayers with assets of $10,000,000 or more and U.S. GAAP certified audited financial statements that elect the Large Business & International (LB&I) ASC 730 Directive on Section E, Line 41 make a single ASC 730 entry in Section G (which does not count toward the 50-component limit; if that entry equals at least 80% of Line 48 QREs, no additional components must be itemized, whereas if it is less than 80%, non-directive components must be listed to reach the 80%/Top 50 threshold). Taxpayers utilizing statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 must still report the 80%/Top 50 business components, append "sample" to the identifier in Column 49(c), and attach Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf.

For each itemized business component, Columns 49(a)–(e) capture the conducting controlled-group member's EIN, principal business activity code, business component name or unique alphanumeric identifier, component type (product, process, or other), and software type if applicable (IUS, Dual Function Software [DFS], Excepted from IUS treatment, or Non-IUS), while Column 49(f) ("Describe the information sought to be discovered") is required solely when claiming a research credit on an amended return. Columns 50 through 53 then disaggregate Qualified Wages across the three statutory service pillars for each component:

Total qualified wages (add line 50, line 51, and line 52)
Sum of Columns 50, 51, and 52 for each business component; the grand total across all reported components (including attachments and Aggregate Business Components) carries to Section F, Line 42.

body.text: Operationally, Section G fundamentally reshapes wage audit selection. Beginning with mandatory reporting for 2026 returns, IRS classifiers receive a component-by-component map exposing the exact ratio of direct supervision (Column 51) and direct support (Column 52) wages relative to hands-on research wages (Column 50) before an examination even opens. Payroll and timekeeping architectures can therefore no longer stop at estimating an employee's annual qualified percentage; they must allocate each employee's strict IRC § 3401(a) wages across discrete business components and tag which of the three functional pillars was performed on each component.
VI. Actionable Compliance Roadmap: Three-Phase Implementation Strategy

Because project and payroll records for tax years beginning in 2026 are generated contemporaneously throughout 2026 ahead of the 2027 filing season, organizations should execute a three-phase compliance roadmap aligned with IRC § 41(b)(2), 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)–(d), federal appellate precedent, and Form 6765 Section G.
A. Phase 1: Implement Contemporaneous, Component-Specific Time and Activity Tracking

items: Define Discrete Business Components Upfront: At the start of the tax year, map engineering product lines, software modules, formulas, and manufacturing process improvements into discrete "Business Components" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B), assigning each a unique alphanumeric identifier matching Form 6765, Section G, Column 49(c) and tagging applicable software categories (Non-IUS, IUS, DFS, or Excepted IUS) for Column 49(e). Establish subcomponent sub-codes for complex systems so the "shrinking-back" rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) remains supported if an overall project fails the four-part test.

Enforce Four-Bucket Functional Time Logging: Bridge engineering workflow platforms (such as Jira, GitHub, or Azure DevOps) with financial ERP timekeeping (such as SAP or Oracle) so employees log hours contemporaneously against specific Business Components across four explicit buckets: (a) Actual Conduct (Column 50), (b) First-Line Direct Supervision (Column 51), (c) Qualifying Direct Support (Column 52, including machinist experimental fabrication, lab equipment cleaning, or research data compilation), and (d) Non-Qualified / Excluded Activities (post-commercial-production maintenance, customer adaptation, routine QA/QC, foreign research outside the U.S./Puerto Rico/U.S. possessions, or general administration).

Segregate Non-Service PTO Hours in Payroll Registers: Configure payroll registers to separately track all paid non-working hours—sick leave, vacation, paid holidays, jury duty, and military leave—so they are systematically excluded from the denominator when computing each employee's Total Service Hours under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) and the IRS June 2005 ATG.

body.text: B. Phase 2: Conduct a Formal 80% Test (Shadow Audit) and Supervisory Role Review

items: Run Mid-Year QSR Shadow Simulations: Prior to year-end, extract year-to-date qualified hours and total active service hours (excluding non-service PTO) for every R&D-participating employee to calculate their projected Qualified Services Ratio (QSR) on an individual employee-by-employee basis under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2).

Optimize Duties for Near-Cliff Personnel (70.0%–79.9% QSR): Identify specialized engineers and scientists whose projected QSR sits between 70.0% and 79.9%. Where operationally appropriate, shifting routine administrative, scheduling, or post-production support duties away from these individuals allows them to legitimately cross the 80.0% active-service threshold, qualifying 100% of their annual IRC § 3401(a) wages for the credit year.

Audit Organizational Hierarchies and Section E, Line 38 Officer Disclosures: Cross-check organizational charts against actual daily duties to ensure Column 51 Direct Supervision claims are restricted to immediate, first-line managers who directly supervise hands-on researchers, excluding second-line directors or VPs. For any state-law corporate officers whose direct research or first-line supervision wages are claimed on Line 42 and disclosed on Section E, Line 38, compile contemporaneous technical calendars, design reviews, and code/experiment logs—and verify compensation reasonableness under IRC § 174(e)—to sustain executive claims upon audit.

body.text: C. Phase 3: Integrate Payroll Extraction with Contemporaneous Technical Narratives (Nexus Defense)

items: Reconcile Strict IRC § 3401(a) Payroll Figures: Configure payroll extraction scripts to pull exact Chapter 24 withholding wages per employee rather than gross labor or unadjusted W-2 Box 1 totals—verifying exclusion of employer 401(k)/retirement contributions (§ 3401(a)(12)), pre-tax 401(k) deferrals (§ 402(e)(3)), pre-tax IRC § 125 cafeteria plan deductions, non-taxable § 132 fringe benefits, imputed group-term life insurance exceeding $50,000 (§ 3401(a)(14)), post-2004 ISO/ESPP disqualifying disposition spreads (§ 421(b) / § 423(c)), and IRC § 51(a) Work Opportunity Credit wages (§ 41(b)(2)(D)(iii)). For any NSO exercise spreads included in exercise-year wages, retain grant-year QSR documentation substantiating that the employee performed qualified services in the grant year per Apple Computer and the 2005 IRS ATG, and reconcile claimed QREs with IRC § 174A capitalization/deduction choices and the IRC § 280C(c) election on Form 6765, Item A.

Screen Client Agreements for Funded Research Risk: Before claiming wages for engineering, architectural, or custom development work performed under third-party contracts, review agreements under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2) to verify both that payment is contingent on research success (Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, 100 F.4th 986) and that the taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research results (Smith v. Commissioner, 2026).

Link Component Wage Schedules to Contemporaneous Experimentation Evidence: To satisfy the standards enforced in Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), and the May 2008 RCCATG, link every business component's Columns 50–53 wage schedule to contemporaneous primary evidence captured as the work occurred—initial documentation of capability, method, or design uncertainties, technical hypotheses formulated, iterative design or code commits evaluated, and simulation/test results—demonstrating that at least 80% of the component's research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6). For any amended-return refund claims, attach full CCM 20214101F sufficiency schedules (including Section G, Column 49(f) descriptions when filing via Form 6765) at the time of filing ahead of the January 10, 2027 transition deadline.
